structure.title: The Window
structure.text: A single day moves among the household's perceptions and expectations.

structure.title: Time Passes and The Lighthouse
structure.text: Years change the scale before the narrative returns to interrupted intentions. Pace matters as much as events.

people.name: Mrs Ramsay
people.text: A beautiful, warm woman in her fifties, mother of eight, who spends a holiday in Scotland arranging guests, meals and marriages around her.

people.name: Mr Ramsay
people.text: An eminent philosopher who fears his work will not last, and who needs his wife and his guests to reassure him.

people.name: Lily Briscoe
people.text: An unmarried painter staying with the Ramsays, who is trying to finish a picture of Mrs Ramsay and her son while being told women can't paint.

context.title: Moving between minds
context.text: The narration slips between people's perceptions without always announcing the change. A description may belong to someone's mood rather than to an impartial observer.
context.takeaway: Ask whose perception colours the sentence.

context.title: Women's work
context.text: Hospitality and painting both involve making something valuable, but receive different kinds of recognition. Woolf puts domestic expectations beside the difficulty of becoming an artist.

notice.why: One destination carries different hopes for different people.

notice.text: Notice meals, objects, and unfinished work.
notice.why: They carry memories that the characters cannot simply recover.

opening: A boy wants to visit a lighthouse, his mother says they might, and his father announces that the weather will be bad. The hurt lasts far longer than the exchange. Around them, guests talk, a painter struggles with her picture, and Mrs Ramsay works to make an evening hold together. Woolf follows the thoughts nobody quite manages to say, before years pass through the house and leave the survivors trying to recover what they scarcely knew they possessed.
